title: multiplication and division facts to 100 (introductory computational strategies)

lesson.title: Multiplication Made Easy: Equal Groups, Skip Counting, and Doubling

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine your class is having a bake sale at school here in B.C. You carry out four trays of muffins, and each tray holds six muffins. You could point at every single muffin and count one, two, three... but that takes forever, and it's easy to lose your place. There's a faster way, and that's what multiplication is for.

visual.caption: Four trays, six muffins on each tray

steps.say: Here's the big idea. When the groups are all the same size, you don't have to count one by one. Six plus six plus six plus six is the same as four groups of six. We write that as four times six, and it equals twenty-four. Multiplication is just a shortcut for adding the same number over and over.

visual.caption: Four equal bars of six make twenty-four

steps.say: Now let's find the fastest helper of all: skip counting. Look at this hundred chart. If I count by fives, I say five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, forty, forty-five, fifty. Do you see how the circles march down in two neat lines? Those numbers are exactly the answers to the five times table, in order. Skip counting by twos, fives, and tens is like a secret map to your multiplication facts.

visual.caption: Counting by fives makes a pattern you can see

steps.say: Let's try a real one. At the farmers market, a basket of B.C. blueberries costs five dollars. Your family buys eight baskets. How much money is that? Eight groups of five. Skip count with me: five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, thirty, thirty-five, forty. So eight times five equals forty dollars. See how you never had to count one dollar at a time?

visual.caption: Eight baskets, five dollars each, forty dollars in all

steps.say: Here's another clever trick called doubling. Say you want four times seven, but you're not sure. Start with something easy: two times seven is fourteen. Now four is just double two, so the answer is double fourteen. Fourteen plus fourteen is twenty-eight. So four times seven is twenty-eight. Whenever you know your twos, you can double your way to your fours.

visual.caption: Double the twos to get the fours

steps.say: Let's use doubling on a slightly bigger one. Your teacher is setting up the library shelf with four rows, and nine books go in each row. Two times nine is eighteen. Double eighteen: eighteen plus eighteen is thirty-six. So four times nine equals thirty-six books. Look at the picture — four rows of nine really does fill thirty-six squares.

visual.caption: Four rows of nine squares equals thirty-six

steps.say: Now here's my favourite part. Multiplication and division are best friends — they live in the same little family. If four rows of nine make thirty-six books, then thirty-six books shared into four equal rows gives nine in each row. And thirty-six shared into groups of nine gives four groups. Knowing one fact hands you three more for free!

visual.caption: Thirty-six shared into four equal groups: nine each

steps.say: So remember: you don't need to memorize everything today. Make equal groups, skip count by twos, fives, and tens, and double when you get stuck. Every time you practise, these facts will pop into your head a little faster. You're doing great!

lesson.answer: Multiplication is just equal groups — skip count or double to find the answer, and every times fact gives you a division fact for free.

practice.question: You're packing snacks for a hike at Stanley Park. Each box of granola bars holds 5 bars, and you pack 7 boxes. How many granola bars is that altogether? Then, if you share all those bars equally among 5 friends, how many does each friend get?
practice.answer: 7 times 5 equals 35 bars (skip count: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35). Shared among 5 friends, 35 divided by 5 equals 7 bars each.
